newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Plan keeps Portugal on track for euro - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Plan keeps Portugal on track for euro - analysts.

text.p: Portugal's Convergence Plan for 1998-2000 keeps the country on course to join the euro in 1999 and has reassured financial markets about the government's commitment to meeting EMU targets, analysts said.
They said the plan, which the government approved last week, underlines its pledge to maintain tight control of state spending, maintain a stable escudo and guarantee moderate wage rises.

"There are no inconsistencies in Portugal's Convergence Plan, which fits in with the government's pledge to join Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and the stability pact," said Jose Luiz Alzola, analyst of Salomon Brothers in London.

Nuno Godinho of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Lisbon said: "There is a strong level of commitment by the government to join EMU. This Convergence Plan is another way of reassuring the markets that the right policies will be carried out."
Martin Amaral Neto, analyst at Portuguese bank Banco Essi, said: "This plan is a way of calming the markets and will have a positive effect in the long term."
The Convergence Plan foresees a budget deficit of 2.9 percent of Gross Domestic Product this year, 2.5 percent in 1998, 2.0 percent in 1999 and 1.5 percent in 2000.
It projects the ratio of public debt to GDP to stand at 64.0 percent this year, 62.5 percent in 1998, 61.0 percent in 1999 and 59.4 percent in 2000.

"The budget deficit target could be a little optimistic, but the intention to reduce the deficit is positive, and gives room for the three percent target to be reached if there were a recession," said Rui Martins dos Santos, chief economist of Banco Portugues de Investimento.

Amaral Neto said the cut in the budget deficit depended not only on efforts to crack down on tax evasion, but also on the containment of state spending and the continuation of reforms in health, social security and the civil service.

The government expects primary current spending, which excludes capital spending including debt interest payments, to stabilise at 35.7 percent of GDP in 1997 and 1998 before dropping to 35.4 percent in 1999 and 35.2 percent in 2000.
The Convergence Plan highlights the government's commitment to maintain a stable escudo and to contain wage increases in the public sector.

"The inflation goals of the Convergence Plan show very clearly that the government does not believe that the escudo will weaken in the two years before the launch of EMU," said one analyst with an investment bank.
Dos Santos said: "Considering the need to keep down inflation, it is essential for the escudo to remain steady or to strengthen slightly and it is vital for imported inflation not to increase."
The escudo has depreciated against the mark in nominal terms by 0.65 percent since the start of the month when it traded at around 100.00 per mark.
Since the last re-alignment of the escudo against the mark on March 6 1995, the escudo has risen in nominal terms by 4.5 percent against the mark.
"For inflation to fall further, there will have to be moderation in wage increases," said Amaral Neto.
Alzola said: "This year salaries are growing at a relatively moderate rate, by an average of about 3.5 percent, compared with 4.5 percent in 1996."

The National Statistics Institute said that salaries grew by 3.7 percent year-on-year in both January and February, which permitted a drop in non-tradeable goods prices and consolidated a downward trend in inflation.
